name: Cerebellar hemispheres (lateral zone)
summary: The lateral zones of the cerebellum, the neocerebellum, expanded enormously with the cerebral cortex and are wired to it: the contralateral motor and association cortices project through the pontine nuclei and middle cerebellar peduncle, and the hemispheres reply through the dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle and thalamus to the same cortex. They plan and time skilled limb movements, particularly of the hand and of speech, and lesions produce the classic ipsilateral limb signs: dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and rebound.

anatomy.location: Lateral to the paravermis on each side, the largest part of the posterior lobe, resting on the occipital bone and the petrous surface; the tonsil is their most medial inferior lobule.

function: Planning and coordination of skilled voluntary movement of the ipsilateral limbs, timing of complex sequences, motor learning, and cognitive-affective functions in the posterior lobe.

imaging.normalAppearance: Striped folia lateral to the vermis; the SCA territory lies above and the PICA territory below the horizontal fissure. Focal lesions are easily missed on axial slices alone; use coronal images.

pathology.finding: Wedge of restricted diffusion in the hemisphere respecting a vascular territory.
Enhancing hemispheric mass with edema; hemangioblastoma is a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in an adult.
FLAIR-bright plaques in the hemispheric white matter or peduncles.

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral limb dysmetria and intention tremor

lesionEffects.mechanism: Posterior lobe lesions: executive, visuospatial and affective changes

examination: Rapid alternating hand movements and heel-shin
Rebound (Holmes) test with the patient's arm outstretched
pearls: Limb ataxia without gait ataxia points to the hemisphere; gait ataxia without limb ataxia points to the vermis
Because of the double crossing, hemispheric lesions produce signs on the same side of the body

citations.section: The surface atlas captures complex folding patterns
Gradient 1 extends from motor to nonmotor areas: cerebellar macroscale organization is sensorimotor-fugal
